name: gnu-units
why: A units converter with a surprisingly large built-in database of physical constants and odd units, fun to explore in a pinch.

brief.what_it_is: GNU Units is a command-line converter for quantities between systems of measurement. You give it a quantity with a unit (for example "mile") and a target unit, and it prints the multiplicative factor both ways. It also handles nonlinear conversions such as Fahrenheit to Celsius and wire gauge, and sums of units such as feet plus inches. Beyond conversion, it works as a scientific calculator that tracks units through expressions with sums, products, quotients, powers and roots. Units are defined in an external data file that ships with the program, and users can supply their own or add to the standard one.
brief.why_it_exists: The page frames it as a converter that can also keep dimensional consistency in long calculations, so mixed units do not silently go wrong. The author describes it as handling conversions that simple multiplicative tools cannot, such as affine temperature scales.
brief.how_it_works: Units are defined as entries in a text data file (the README says the definitions are generally found in /usr/share/units/). The program reads that file, so the unit vocabulary can be extended or replaced without changing the program. Expressions are checked for dimensional consistency as they are evaluated, which is how it can report results like a definition in K from an expression involving W/m^2 and the Stefan-Boltzmann constant.

brief.install_notes: The homepage points to source tarballs on the GNU FTP server (http://ftp.gnu.org/gnu/units/, or a GNU mirror) and a Windows binary at http://ftp.gnu.org/gnu/units/windows/, maintained separately by Jeff Conrad. The page does not give a version number or build steps. The Homebrew metadata given to me says the installed commands carry a g prefix (gunits and gunits_cur), with a gnubin directory available on PATH if you want the plain names; that comes from the brew metadata, not from the README.
brief.standout: Most converters are lookup tables with a multiplier. This one treats units as a small algebra: it does dimensional arithmetic, accepts sums like 17 yards + 2 feet + 5 inches, and can output sums like 22 ft + 11.590551 in. The data file is also an external, editable text file, so the built-in list of odd units and constants is something you can read and extend.
brief.status: Maintained, with light evidence. The page names Adrian Mariano as current maintainer for bug reports and feature requests, and the page was updated 2024/12/02. The page does not show a software release date or version, so I could not check recent release activity.
brief.caveats: The homepage does not state a version or release date. Build steps and platform details beyond the Windows binary are not on the page; I did not open the README in the source tarball or the manual. The Windows binary is maintained separately from the main release. The licence is GPL version 3 or later.

judge.reason: It turns unit conversion into dimensional algebra, catching inconsistent calculations while exposing an editable trove of physical constants and unusual units.

entry.title: GNU Units
entry.tldr: A unit converter that treats units as algebra, tracking dimensions through whole expressions, with a big editable text file of odd units and constants behind it.
entry.deeper_look:
GNU Units converts a quantity in one system of measurement to another. Give it a quantity such as a mile and a target unit, and it prints the multiplier in both directions. It also handles conversions a plain multiplier cannot, such as Fahrenheit to Celsius and wire gauge, and it accepts sums of units like feet plus inches.

Underneath, it is a small calculator that keeps track of units through sums, products, quotients, powers and roots. Expressions are checked for dimensional consistency as they are evaluated, so mixed units do not silently go wrong in a long calculation. That is the idea worth taking away: units are a type system for physical quantities, and a tool can enforce it.

The vocabulary is not hard-coded. Units are defined in an external text data file that ships with the program (the README says the definitions are generally found in /usr/share/units/). You can read it, add your own definitions, or supply a whole different file. Browsing that file is a good way to find out which strange units and constants someone thought worth writing down.
entry.install:
brew install gnu-units
# Homebrew installs the commands with a g prefix (gunits, gunits_cur). For the plain name `units`, add to your shell rc:
# PATH="$HOMEBREW_PREFIX/opt/gnu-units/libexec/gnubin:$PATH"
